title: Thomas Coyle drowned off Cuan bheag
summary: A westerly storm on the second night of an t-Sultain drowns eleven Tuathaich fishermen out of Cuan bheag, Thomas Coyle of Caol mhòr among them, one-and-forty and near twenty years married to Mary Coyle. The sea gives back two broken hulls and a stranger's oar; the town buries what it can within the week.

title: Mary Coyle's roll of the eleven dead
summary: Mary Coyle, newly widowed, writes the eleven drowned men's names out on a single sheet for the mason's stones, setting them in the order the boats went out rather than the order the sea gave the bodies back, holding that order the truer one.

title: Tional nan Tuathach opens its lifeboat subscription
summary: Walter Hale carries the wreck's news to Tional nan Tuathach's own council at Caol mhòr, which votes that same evening to open a subscription for a lifeboat at Cuan bheag; Hale opens the list himself, and it carries near two hundred names by the month's end. The council, asked to bear half the cost, answers four months on that it will bear a third.

title: The Cuan bheag lifeboat launched
summary: The lifeboat ordered of the Cuan shean yard comes up the coast in an Cèitean and is set afloat off Cuan bheag's jetty by the hands of that autumn's five widows, no priest of either faith having an agreed form to bless a boat neither had built.

title: The tale of Uilebheist na Mara told to the chronicler
summary: A fisherman out of Achadh àrsaidh, at the summer bothies below the cold cape, tells Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill the coast's own tale of a shape seen off the cold cape, seen always at a distance and never named by those who fear it, which she enters in the book that keeps what people said rather than the book that keeps names.

title: The raiders' anchorage noted at the cold cape
summary: The same fisherman tells Gormshuil that Na Longan gun Bhratach working those waters know the cold cape's currents better than any stranger crew should, and keep some hidden anchorage among its rocks; she writes it apart from the tale and asks that the council's coastal watch be told of it.

title: The flocks of Eilean dhubh counted by their own hands
summary: A treasury clerk sent to number the flocks of Eilean dhubh for the head-due finds the islanders unwilling to have him count their own pastures, and takes instead their sworn count by tally-stick, on which the island's dues are set that year and every year after.

title: Nell Barrow's first letter for Cathair gheal
summary: Nell Barrow, a skipper's widow of Cathair gheal who has lost a nephew to the raiders, writes the town's case to the council in am Faoilleach, asking a boat armed at the council's expense or leave to arm the town's own; the maor warns her plain words are as likely filed as answered. No answer comes.

title: Nell Barrow's second letter for Cathair gheal
summary: Two months unanswered, Nell Barrow writes a second letter in am Màrt, shorter and plainer than the first, ending that the town does not think a third asking will find the council less occupied than the first two were. It too goes unanswered.

title: The black ship run aground in Cathair gheal's bay
summary: On the night of 8 an Giblean three flagless hulls stand into Cathair gheal's bay; the largest raider ship runs her keel onto a shifted bar and is boarded and burned by seven town boats before dawn, the two lesser hulls standing off rather than come to her aid.

title: Two dead and four hurt in the bay's clearing
summary: The fight for Cathair gheal's bay costs the town two men dead and four hurt, one of whom keeps no further use of a hand; Nell Barrow herself takes a burn from a fallen lantern that scars her the rest of her life, and by first light tells the town the bay is clear.

title: Cathair gheal fined for bearing arms unlicensed
summary: The council's ruling on the night's fight names no boat sent and no licence granted, only that Cathair gheal bore arms without leave first asked, and fines the town four purses of Bonn na Rìoghachd, to be paid at the maor's own office before the year's dues fall due.

title: Walter Hale carries Tional nan Tuathach's purse north to Cathair gheal
summary: Hearing the town lacks two-thirds of its fine, Walter Hale carries the difference north from Tional nan Tuathach's own purse, the same purse the Cuan bheag lifeboat has already thinned, and reaches Cathair gheal near the end of an t-Iuchar.

title: The fine paid at the maor's door
summary: Nell Barrow's sum and Hale's together clear the fine in full at the maor's own door, counted coin by coin before his clerk, who enters the sum received and asks nothing of the six years, the two letters, or the boat the town was never sent.

title: The eleven stones set at Cuan bheag
summary: The mason of Cuan bheag cuts and sets eleven stones for the drowned from Mary Coyle's single sheet, in the order the boats went out, and they stand weathering by the jetty when the lifeboat is put into the water the spring after.

title: Ellen Hale dies at Caol mhòr
summary: Ellen Hale, Walter Hale's wife, dies at Caol mhòr in the second week of an Lùnastal at seventy, in the loft the family had lodged in since the boat brought them north; Tional nan Tuathach's day-book gives the day and the hour, and beneath them David's line that Tional nan Tuathach did not sit that week.

title: Ellen Hale buried on the rise above the harbour
summary: Ellen Hale is buried on the rise above Caol mhòr's harbour with the fishwives, the Carrick women, the widows of the Cuan bheag drowning and the whole of Tional nan Tuathach's council standing by; the minister reads the twenty-third psalm, from which she had taught her children their letters, and her husband says nothing aloud.

title: Crosses and lifeboats
summary: Hearing the council's long minute on the Mac Ùisdein market cross read at Tional nan Tuathach's table beside its short one on Cathair gheal's fine, Mary Coyle says that the council seems to know a great deal about crosses and rather less about lifeboats, and goes back to counting the boats home.
